title: Variability in ADHD Symptoms Throughout the Menstrual Cycle in Women of Reproductive Age: A Comparison of the Mid-Follicular Phase and the Late Luteal Phase
summary:
Background
Many women with ADHD only realise at a late stage – often not until adulthood – that their problems with concentration, inner restlessness or mood swings are due to a neurobiological difference. This is primarily because ADHD manifests differently in girls and women than in boys and men. Whilst boys often stand out in childhood due to their behaviour (e.g. fidgeting or acting impulsively), girls and women frequently display internal symptoms such as:

severe emotional fluctuations,
difficulties concentrating,
internal restlessness rather than motor hyperactivity,
or a constant effort to conceal their difficulties (masking).

These symptoms are often misinterpreted as stress, depression or anxiety disorders – rather than ADHD. Furthermore, the menstrual cycle may play an additional role: for many women, hormonal fluctuations affect mood, concentration and stress responses. However, this influence has so far received little attention in ADHD research.
Another problem is that ADHD has long been classified as a typically male disorder. Most studies and diagnostic procedures were developed and validated using boys and men. This means that the classic ADHD criteria (e.g. hyperactivity as motor restlessness) do not always apply to women. Many women with ADHD are therefore diagnosed late, if at all – with serious consequences:

They struggle for years with vague symptoms,
develop further conditions such as depression or anxiety disorders, or are treated incorrectly because their symptoms go unrecognised.

It is only in recent years that research has begun to focus more closely on the gender-specific aspects of ADHD. However, there is still a lack of evidence regarding how symptoms in women change throughout the menstrual cycle and whether this should be taken into account in diagnosis.

Key research question:
Do symptoms in women with attention deficit disorders vary more significantly across the two phases of the menstrual cycle than in women without such disorders?

Further research questions:

Impulsivity: Which forms of impulsivity (e.g. acting on impulse, emotional overreactions) are particularly pronounced – and do they change over the course of the menstrual cycle?

Emotional regulation: How well can you control your emotions – and does this ability change during the different phases of the cycle?

Traumatic childhood experiences: Did the participants experience any difficult events during their childhood (e.g. neglect, violence)?

Premenstrual symptoms: How severe are your physical and emotional symptoms?

Masking (camouflaging): To what extent do you try to hide or compensate for ADHD symptoms in everyday life, and is there a link to the phase of the cycle?

Methodology:

Women with natural menstrual cycles, both with and without ADHD, will complete a total of five online self-report questionnaires over a period of up to 12 weeks. The women will be asked by email to complete the questionnaires at specific points in their cycle.

interventions.name:
The study includes two arms with longitudinal data collection over two menstrual cycles. Each participant completes a screening questionnaire (T0) and then undergoes four measurement points (two per cycle phase; T1–T4) with questionnaires administered at various time points.

Arm 1: Women with ADH

Each participant completes a screening questionnaire (T0) and then undergoes four measurement points (two per cycle phase; T1–T4) with questionnaires administered at various time points.

Arm 2:  the control group comprising healthy women without ADHD

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
For all participants
-    People who menstruate, are aged 18 or older and have a good knowledge of German
-    The participant fully understands all the information provided and voluntarily gives her consent to take part in the study

For the ADHD group
-    A diagnosis of ADHD issued by a qualified professional, or a suspicion that ADHD symptoms are present
Exclusion criteria:
for all participants
-    People who are under 18 years of age and do not have a good knowledge of German
-    Women with an irregular menstrual cycle (duration <25; >35 days) (Schmalenberger et al., 2021)
-    Use of certain hormonal contraceptives that suppress ovulation: combined hormonal contraceptives such as the combined oral contraceptive pill, the patch and the vaginal ring; also the contraceptive injection and the hormonal coil (except Jaydess (see Jaydess patient information leaflet)), as well as current hormone therapy or diagnosed hormonal disorders (if a regular cycle is not desired)
-    If hormonal methods have been used previously, a wash-out period of at least two natural cycles is absolutely essential (Schmalenberger et al., 2021).
-    Pregnancy or breastfeeding (at least three regular cycles should have occurred since weaning) (Schmalenberger et al., 2021)

for the ADHD group
-    Changes in ADHD-related therapy, intervention or medication during data collection
